Seminar Title:

Development of a High-Capacity Modular AB5 Metal Hydride Reactor for SolidState Hydrogen Storage in Fuel Cell Applications

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Mechanical Engineering

Speaker Name:

Sreeraj R ( Rollno : 519me6018)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

ME Seminar Hall [ME001]

Date and Time:

03 Nov 2026 09.30 AM

Contact:

S. Anbarasu

Abstract:

This thesis investigates the design, fabrication, and experimental characterisation of a high-capacity, modular, solid-state hydrogen storage system using LaNi4.8Sn0.2 as the hydride material. A critical review of the existing literature revealed several underexplored areas: the absence of standardised reactor performance parameters, limited comparative studies across reactor configurations, underdeveloped hybrid heat exchanger designs, insufficient large-scale experimental work under realistic operating conditions, and poor integration of reactor design with application-specific performance requirements.

LaNi4.8Sn0.2 was selected as the storage alloy following a thorough review of AB5-type metal hydrides. According to the literature, partial substitution of Ni by Sn was found to preserve the CaCu5-type hexagonal crystal structure while expanding the unit cell volume by 2.47%, with consequent improvements in thermodynamic stability and sorption kinetics. The physical properties and thermal behaviour of the alloy were measured and reported. Gas-phase absorption and desorption measurements on a 62 kg hydride bed yielded the maximum hydrogen storage capacity of 1.35 wt.%.

Parametric absorption experiments on the 62 kg modular reactor examined the influence of supply pressure, HTF temperature, flow rate, and hydride filling capacity. At 5 bar, 25&degC, and 20 LPM, the reactor stored 788 g of hydrogen (1.21 wt.%) in 6829.8 s (113.83 min). Raising the hydrogen supply pressure to 30 bar increased storage capacity by 10.97% (875.3 g) and reduced absorption time by 66.49% (2288.6 s or 38.13 min), with a peak bed temperature of 101.2&degC. At 20 bar and 15&degC HTF temperature, 886.8 g was absorbed in 3578 s (59.63 min), with a maximum bed temperature of 73.3&degC. At 80% fill capacity,
30 bar, and 15&degC, hydrogen uptake increased to 1005.05 g in 2708.4 s (45.14 min). A cooling jacket contributed a marginal 0.3% gain in absorption capacity.

Desorption experiments across 10-90&degC showed equilibrium-limited behaviour at lower temperatures, with hydrogen releases of 47.8 g, 68.6 g, and 98.3 g at 10, 20, and 30&degC, respectively. Beyond 70&degC, recovery exceeded 90% of storage capacity, and the average desorption rate increased from 0.029 g&middots⁻1 at 40&degC to 0.099 g&middots⁻1 at 90&degC. At 80&degC, the controlled desorption study increased the hydrogen withdrawal rate, reduced desorption time from 12.04 h to 1.67 h, consistent with a shift in the rate-limiting step from solid-state diffusion to gas-phase mass transport. The findings demonstrate the practical feasibility of a solid-state hydrogen storage system at scale, with direct relevance to fuel cell integration and stationary energy applications.
